now.downWhy: Gone from the wall, the catalogue, search and the direct address. The owner sees it marked as taken down, with your reason, and cannot put it back.
now.parkedWhy: The owner took it off the wall themselves. Nothing to do with you, and they can put it back whenever they like.
now.codeWhy: Published, but it opens only for someone who has the code. It is on the wall; the contents are not.
now.seoWhy: Either you blocked it or this site offers nothing to search engines. The app is otherwise completely normal.
now.neverWhy: Published and never opened once. Worth a look before the wall fills up with them.

menu.seoBlock: Keep it out of search engines
menu.seoAllow: Offer it to search engines again
menu.takeDown: Take it down, with a reason

scan.title: Copies and watermarks
scan.lead: Two different things, and only one of them is evidence. A watermark hit means this site served one app to a named person and another app now carries that exact fingerprint. A close pair is a signal: two apps whose bytes are alike with no fork link between them, which a shared template explains as easily as a copy does.
scan.notYet: Not scanned yet. The scan reads every app's bytes, so it takes a few seconds and runs only when you ask.
scan.noEvidence: No watermark from one app was found inside another.
scan.noSignal: No two apps are alike enough to mention.
scan.sameOwner: Same owner ({who}), so this is most likely their own work reused.
scan.differentOwners: Different owners, and no fork link between them.
scan.theOriginal: The one it was served from
scan.unknownOwner: not on this site any more

states.title: Four ways an app can be off the wall
states.lead: They look alike on a list and mean entirely different things. Only the first is yours.
states.downWhy: Gone from the wall, the catalogue, search and its own address. The owner sees it marked as taken down, with your reason, and cannot put it back.
states.parkedWhy: Their own decision, and theirs to undo. It keeps its address for anyone who has the link.
states.codeWhy: On the wall and in search, but it opens only for someone who has the code the owner set.
states.seo: Search engines are not told about it
states.seoWhy: Either you blocked it or this site offers nothing to search engines. The app is otherwise completely normal.
states.dangerLabel: The one action that cannot be undone
states.danger: Deleting removes the app, its versions and its screenshot from this site for good, and the owner is not asked. It lives in the row menu behind the three dots, with the filename to type. Taking an app down does everything a mistake needs and can be undone in one press.

apps.hideExplain: It goes from the wall, the catalogue, search and its own address. The owner keeps their copy, sees it marked as taken down, and cannot put it back. You can, in one press.
apps.reasonPh: Copies another app without a fork link
apps.deleteWarn: The app, every version of it and its screenshot go from this site, and the owner is not asked and loses their copy. If you only want it off the wall, take it down instead: that is undone in one press.

security.title: Security
security.intro: What this instance turned away at the door, what it refused and kept for you to look at, and the settings that decide both. A count is for the last 24 hours unless its row says since the restart.
security.loadFailed: The security page could not be read just now. It is served at /v1/admin/security/overview.
security.deleteConfirm: Delete this incident and its quarantined file?

now.title: Right now
now.lineQuiet: No open incidents or unusual levels were detected in the readable sample.
now.lineWatch: Nothing is open, but one number sits above its usual level; the rows say which.
now.lineUnknown: There is not enough readable history to assess the refusal rate.
now.lineOpenOne: An incident is open and waits for you in section 03.
now.lineOpenMany: {n} incidents are open and wait for you in section 03.
now.lineWalledOne: One address, {source}, hit the wall at a credential door {n} times in the last 24 hours.
now.lineWalledMany: {sources} addresses hit the wall at a credential door {n} times in the last 24 hours.
now.logOn: Refusal log on · rotates at {mb} MB
now.refusalsWhy: Observed 401/403 responses in up to 1,000 readable log lines, filtered to the last 24 hours. The full daily total is unknown.
now.refusalsMean: mean {mean} a day over {hours} readable hours
now.refusalsNoMean: insufficient history to assess the rate
now.sourcesWhy: Distinct addresses refused. Many sources with a few tries each is a scan passing through; one source with many is a script or a person.
now.rateLimitWhy: Requests slowed or dropped for arriving too fast, all doors together. The limits are tuned under Settings, group Rate limits.
now.scopeWhy: A real credential that lacked the word for the door. Usually an agent whose owner narrowed it; the agent is told which word to ask for.
now.openWhy: Refused uploads kept for inspection. An open one waits for you to look at the bytes and resolve it; section 03 has them.

refusals.title: Who was turned away
refusals.lead: The latest {n} lines. Groupings use a sample of up to 1,000 readable lines filtered to the last 24 hours; the daily total is unknown.
refusals.disabled: The refusal log is switched off. Set a file path in the environment (AIMEAT_AUTH_LOG_PATH) and restart.
refusals.none: Nothing has been refused since the log started.
refusals.noneInWindow: Nothing was refused in the last 24 hours.
refusals.fingerprint: One fingerprint, {digest}, is {count} of the {total} refusals with a {kind}: a script somewhere still holds a credential that no longer works.
refusals.fingerprint403: One fingerprint, {digest}, is {count} of the {total} refusals with a {kind}: a real credential reaching for doors it may not open, which is a misconfigured integration or somebody testing the fence.
refusals.search: a door, a source, a fingerprint or a name
refusals.note: {shown} of up to 1 000 readable lines · {window} in the last 24 h

incidents.title: Refused and kept
incidents.lead: An upload that failed a safety check was refused, and when it was small enough the bytes were kept for you to look at. Resolve it once you have; delete it to drop the bytes as well.
incidents.none: Nothing has been refused and kept.
incidents.noneOpen: Nothing is open. The last incident was resolved on {date}.

accounts.title: Accounts and roles
accounts.operatorsOne: One person holds the operator role
accounts.operatorsWhy: {names}. An operator can deactivate any account but their own, and take a lost second factor off an account.
accounts.deactivatedNoneWhy: Deactivating stops every credential in an account's name at once; the account and its knowledge stay. It is done from Owners.
accounts.deactivatedWhy: {list}. Every credential in that name stopped then; the account and its knowledge stayed.
accounts.twoStep: Two-step sign-in is on for {n} of {total} accounts
accounts.twoStepWhy: The rest sign in with a password alone. The switch is theirs, on their own Access page; from here you can only remove a lost factor.
accounts.ssoOnWhy: A connected directory can create accounts here and end them.
accounts.ssoOffWhy: No directory is connected, so accounts are made here. Turning it on lets a company's own directory create and end them.
accounts.registrationWhy: The modes are open, sign-in providers only, invitation only, and closed.

settings.title: The doors' settings
settings.lead: The settings that decide what happens at a door, read as sentences. Change any of them under Settings; the search there finds the row by these names.
settings.loginWhy: Past that the door answers 429 for the rest of the window.
settings.tarpitWhy: {free} refusals cost nothing; each one after adds {step} s, held at most {max} s; after {block} the door refuses without trying. A penalty decays in {decay} quiet minutes.
settings.tarpitOffWhy: Repeated credential failures from one address are not slowed down.
settings.lockoutWhy: The account, not the address: a lockout is what the person sees, whoever caused it.
settings.registrationWhy: Admin setup answers the same way, {admin} {window}.
settings.totpWhy: Issuer {issuer}, {codes} backup codes; {failed} wrong codes lock it for {minutes} minutes.
settings.passkeysWhy: A passkey is a way in of its own, beside the password.
settings.corsWhy: Browsers on other origins are refused before any door is asked.

federation.specific_peers: Federated sign-in: the peers you name

settings.federationWhy: Whether people from peer instances can sign in here, and which peers count.
settings.body: Request bodies: {mb} MB, {large} MB for apps and extensions
settings.bodyWhy: A larger body is refused before it is read.
settings.logWhy: {path}, {bytes} of {max}; rotates past that and keeps one older generation.
settings.logOffWhy: Nothing is written when somebody is turned away. Set a file path to keep the story.

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: The paste
ai.lead: Your own AI can read this page and act on the levers, through MCP: read what is here, tell one dead token from somebody guessing, resolve an incident, deactivate or reactivate an account, and remove a lost second factor. It proposes; you say yes.

now.title: Right now
now.line: The active extensions add {actions} HTTP actions to this instance. Nothing here calls {idle} of them, and no clock wakes them.
now.actionsWhy: Each action is an HTTP route under /v1/ext/<extension>/<action>, open to any caller that holds the scope it asks for
now.called: Called by an app or a cortex
now.calledWhy: Something on this instance declares that it needs the extension. Uninstalling it breaks that.
now.clockWhy: A schedule in the manifest wakes the extension on its own, whether or not anything calls it
now.idle: Called by nothing, on no clock
now.idleWhy: No app, no cortex and no schedule. An agent can still call the actions directly, and that is not counted here.
now.offWhy: Installed and inactive: its actions answer 404 until it is switched back on
now.instancesWhy: An extension can declare that it runs as several configured copies, each with its own settings

list.title: Installed
list.findPlaceholder: A name, a description, an app
list.note: Called by is read from what each app and cortex declares it needs. An agent calling /v1/ext/… directly does not appear there, so a row that says nothing means nothing on this instance names it.

ext.calledByWhy: Read from what each app and cortex declares it needs. Uninstalling this stops them.
ext.calledByNothingWhy: No app and no cortex declares this one. An agent calling its actions directly would not show up here.

f.asksWhy: the parts of ctx the manifest declares; the sandbox hands it nothing else
f.storageWhy: its own namespace: anyone may read it, only this extension may write it

ext.switchOffWhy: Switching off leaves it installed and answers 404 on its actions. Its stored data is kept.
ext.switchOnWhy: Switching on makes its actions answer again, with the data it had.
ext.uninstallAsk: Uninstall {name}? Its actions stop answering and its stored data goes with it.
ext.uninstallAskUsed: Uninstall {name}? These stop working: {list}. Its stored data goes with it.

inst.title: Instances
inst.none: No instances. The extension supports them; none has been created.
inst.removeAsk: Remove the instance {id}? Its own stored data goes with it.
inst.createWhy: An id that is yours to choose. It appears in the action route in place of :instanceId.

bundled.title: Install one that ships with the release
bundled.lead: These come with the release. Installing one copies it in and switches it on, and its actions answer immediately.
bundled.note: Reinstall replaces the installed copy with the one in the release. Settings and anything in the extension's own storage are kept.

write.title: Write a new one
write.lead: Creates the manifest and one empty action, ready to edit. It is installed switched off, so nothing answers until you switch it on.
write.apis: The parts of ctx it asks for
write.sandboxWhy: An outside call goes through the URL check: a private or loopback address is refused and every redirect is checked again. Everything the sandbox refuses is written to the log.
write.ctxLead: Every action runs as a function with one argument, ctx. It returns an object; anything thrown becomes a 500 with the message in the log.
write.step1: Write the action script and save it.
write.step3: Call the action and read the answer.
write.step4: Point an app or a cortex at it, so this page can say what uses it.

ctx.caller: who is calling, as a GAII
ctx.owner: the person whose name the call is made in
ctx.instance: the instance id, when the extension has instances
ctx.memGet: read one key from the extension's own storage
ctx.memList: list the keys under a prefix
ctx.log: one line to the server log

now.title: Right now
now.line: Outgoing mail is relayed through {host}. A failed send is retried three times, at 1, 3 and 9 seconds, and then dropped. There is no queue that survives a restart, and no copy of a message is kept.
now.serverWhy: The server this instance relays its outgoing mail through. Set in the environment and read at start-up.
now.transportWhy: Port 587 opens in plain text and upgrades with STARTTLS. Port 465 is TLS from the first byte. The port and the mode have to match.
now.certificateWhy: Turning it off stops all validation: expiry, hostname and chain. Anyone between this instance and the server can then read the mail. For a self-signed certificate, trust the CA instead.
now.fromWhy: What the recipient sees in the From field, and where a reply goes. A bounce comes back to it too.
now.fromDomainWhy: The receiving side checks SPF and DKIM against this domain. The records live in DNS, not on this page.
now.fromDomainOtherWhy: This domain is not {host}, so the receiving side checks whether SPF and DKIM on it allow that server. Without those DNS records the mail is filtered as spam.
now.credentialsWhy: Read from the environment at start-up. This page shows whether they are set, never their value.
now.verificationWhy: When this is required, a new account must type the code from the verification email before it can be used.

strip.weekSub: sent since this day last week

test.title: Send a test message
test.lead: Sends one real message through the server above, so it checks the connection, the credentials and the From address at once. The reply below is what the SMTP server returned.
test.note: One message, sent immediately. No copy is kept.
test.refused: The server did not accept the message.
test.hintOk: Accepted by the relay. It can still bounce or be filtered later, and neither is visible here.
test.hintBad: Nothing was sent. Check the host, the port and the credentials above, then the log for the server's own words.
test.hintIdle: The result appears here, with what the server said.

auto.title: What this instance sends by itself
auto.lead: Six kinds of message go out automatically. Three of them use a template you can edit below; the other three are written in the code. The last row is the group message from section 04, which is sent by hand.
auto.note: A person receives any of these only if they have a notification address on their account. The counts are lifetime totals from this instance's own counters; the messages themselves are not stored.

when.verification: Someone signs up, or adds an email address to an account
when.magic_link: Someone asks to sign in without a password
when.notification: This instance or an app notifies a person: a new message, a finished job, a pending approval
when.invitation: Someone invites a person who has no account here
when.key_invitation: A workspace hands out an access key to an address
when.key_credentials: An access key is issued and its username and password are sent
when.group_send: An operator sends a message to a group from this page

group.title: Send to a group
group.lead: One message to everyone in the group who has an email address on their account. It goes out as a notification, one message per recipient with no shared To or Cc, and it cannot be recalled.
group.subject: Subject
group.bodyPlaceholder: Plain text. It is wrapped in the notification template.
group.note: Sent one at a time. A recipient the server refuses is skipped and the rest still go.
group.whoHint: The people left out have no email address on their account. They are skipped, and no error is reported.

tpl.title: Templates
tpl.warnLead: Editing a template does not change what goes out yet.
tpl.warn: A saved template is stored here, and every send still uses the version written in the code. Use the editor to write and preview them; it takes effect when sending switches over to saved templates.
tpl.placeholdersWhy: These are replaced with real values when the message is sent. Keep them exactly as they are, in both the HTML and the plain text.
tpl.width: 600 px, the usual width for an email template
tpl.aiPrompt: Copy a prompt for your AI
tpl.aiHint: The prompt includes the current template, its placeholders and the language, so an AI can rewrite it without removing the placeholders. Paste what it gives you into the HTML and the plain text views.
tpl.resetAsk: Drop the saved template and go back to the built-in one for this language?
tpl.seedNote: Copies the built-in template of every type into every language, so there is something to edit.
tpl.reseed: Copy the built-in templates in again
tpl.resetAllAsk: Drop every saved template in every language and go back to the built-in ones?
tpl.seededNote: Saved templates exist. Dropping them all goes back to the built-in ones.
tpl.bothParts: Each template has an HTML part and a plain-text part, and both travel in the same message. A client set to plain text shows the text part.

off.line: No SMTP server is configured, so no mail goes out at all. The list below shows what does not work until one is.
off.verificationWhy: Email addresses cannot be confirmed, so no account can add one
off.magicWhy: Signing in without a password is unavailable. The password still works.
off.notificationWhy: People see notifications in the app; nothing reaches them by email
off.invitesWhy: The invitation is created and the link works, but you have to deliver it yourself
off.setLead: Environment variables, read once at start-up. Set them where this instance's environment is defined, then restart it. Any SMTP server works: your own, or your mail provider's.
off.setNote: The host is what turns email on; the rest tune it. Set the port to match the encryption: 587 with AIMEAT_SMTP_SECURE=false uses STARTTLS, 465 with true is TLS from the first byte. Leave AIMEAT_SMTP_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=true unless you know why not.
off.dnsNote: If the From address is on a different domain than the SMTP server, add SPF and DKIM records for that domain in DNS. Without them the mail is delivered and filtered as spam.

cors.title: CORS
cors.intro: Which browser origins this instance answers: by default, and for the people and agents who keep a list of their own. A request without an Origin header is not a browser and is never asked.
cors.loadFailed: The CORS page could not be read just now. It is served at /v1/admin/cors/overview.
cors.clearConfirm: Clear this list? Everything done in this name answers the default again.

now.title: Right now
now.lineAnyNone: A page on any origin may call this instance in a signed-in name. Nobody keeps a list of their own, so the default is the whole answer.
now.lineAnySome: A page on any origin may call this instance in a signed-in name, except in the names of {who}, where only the origins on their own list are answered.
now.lineNamedNone: Only a page on one of {n} named origins may call this instance in a signed-in name. Nobody keeps a list of their own.
now.lineNamedSome: Only a page on one of {n} named origins may call this instance in a signed-in name, except in the names of {who}, where only their own list is answered.
now.logAny: cors.allowed_origins = * · three cookie doors take no wildcard
now.logAnon: anonymous mode on: a request without a credential is answered from any origin
now.default: Every origin is answered by default
now.defaultWhy: The default list is *. A page anywhere may call this instance in a signed-in name and the answer carries credentials. The browser is told so on its preflight; an origin that is not allowed gets no answer at all, and the browser blocks it.
now.defaultNamedWhy: {list}. A page on any other origin gets no answer at all on its preflight, and the browser blocks it.
now.cookieDoorsWhy: Refresh, revoke and the silent app grant hand back a token on the sign-in cookie, so they answer only an origin named in the default list, never *. None is named, so they are same-origin only, which is what the apex needs.
now.cookieDoorsNamedWhy: Refresh, revoke and the silent app grant hand back a token on the sign-in cookie, so they answer only an origin named in the default list, never *. {n} are named: {list}.
now.people: People with a list of their own
now.peopleWhy: A person's list replaces the default for everything done in their name, by them or by an agent of theirs without a list. Set on their own Access page or here, section 02.
now.agents: Agents with a list of their own
now.agentsWhy: An agent's list beats its owner's, for what the agent does and nothing else. The owner sets it on the agent's page, an operator here, section 03.
now.records: Records with a list of their own
now.recordsWhy: One memory record can name the origins that may read it, set by the agent that owns it. It beats every list above, for that record alone.

people.title: People with their own list
people.lead: Everything done in this person's name answers only these origins, whatever the default says. The person can set the same list on their own Access page; clearing it here puts them back on the default.
people.none: Nobody has a list of their own. All {n} accounts answer the default.

agents.title: Agents with their own list
agents.lead: An agent's list beats its owner's for what the agent does, and only for that. The owner can set it on the agent's page; an operator here. An agent without a list answers its owner's list, or the default.
agents.none: No agent has a list of its own. All {n} answer their owner's list or the default.

form.rule: An origin is a scheme and a host, http(s)://…, or * for every origin. Anything else is refused before it is saved.

order.title: How an origin is decided
order.lead: Four lists, most specific first; the first one that is not empty is the whole answer. The three cookie doors read the default list only, and take no wildcard from anyone.
order.recordWhy: A memory record can name who may read it from a browser, set by the agent that owns it. It wins for that record alone.
order.agentWhy: For everything the agent does. Section 03.
order.personWhy: For everything done in the person's name, by them or by an agent of theirs without a list. Section 02.
order.defaultWhy: Everyone else, and every request that carries no credential. Set under Settings, group CORS, or with the environment variable; {value} today.

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: The paste
ai.lead: Your own AI can read this page and change the lists, through MCP: read what is here, say which list gains nothing and which origin is a leftover, and set or clear a list. It proposes; you say yes.

now.title: Right now
now.lineNone: Eleven moments can call out to your own code, and none of them does. Nothing here changes how this site behaves until you bind something.
now.lineBound: {n} of the eleven call out, {gates} of them before the thing happens.
now.lineFailing: A gate is refusing everything it guards, because {what} is not answering. Clear {hook} or fix the address.
now.whatIsWhy: A moment in this site's life where it stops and calls an address you name, over the internet, and waits for the answer.
now.gatesWhy: A hook whose name starts with pre_ runs BEFORE the thing happens and its answer decides: a registration, a work request, a board post or a new peer can be refused. The other {rest} are told afterwards and cannot stop anything.
now.bindWhatWhy: A published action that carries an address. {n} of the ones here do.
now.bindWhatNone: A published action that carries an address. There are none here yet, so there is nothing to bind until somebody publishes one.
now.whenDown: When your address does not answer
now.whenDownWhy: A gate waits {s} seconds per bound action, in order, and a timeout or an error REFUSES the thing. One unreachable address stops every registration here.
now.lastRanWhy: Every call is recorded: which moment, which address, what it answered and how long it took.

strip.momentsSub: where this site can call you
strip.boundSub: {n} of them before the thing happens

moments.title: The eleven moments
moments.lead: Each row is one moment. A gate runs before the thing happens and its answer decides; the rest are told once it has. Bind an address to a row and this site will call it from then on.
moments.clearConfirm: Clear everything bound to {hook}? It stops calling out.
moments.h_pre_owner_registration: Somebody is about to get an account
moments.w_pre_owner_registration: The name and display name go out before the account exists. Refuse, and they are turned away with your reason.
moments.w_post_owner_registration: The name and the roles it got. Nothing you answer changes anything.
moments.h_pre_agent_registration: An agent is about to be registered
moments.w_pre_agent_registration: Fires on both doors: the device approval a person clicks, and the direct registration. The agent's name and its owner go out.
moments.w_post_agent_registration: Its full identity and its owner.
moments.w_owner_recovery: The account name. Worth watching: this is the door a stolen account would come back through.
moments.w_agent_rekey: The agent and its owner. The same reason as above: a key change is how a taken-over agent is kept.
moments.h_pre_work_request: Work is about to be ordered
moments.w_pre_work_request: Who is ordering what, before any morsels move. Refuse, and the order does not happen.
moments.w_post_work_delivery: The tracking code and both parties.
moments.w_post_settlement: The settled work and what it cost. This is the row a bookkeeping integration wants.
moments.h_pre_board_post: Something is about to be posted on a board
moments.w_pre_board_post: The board and the author, before the post is public. This is where a house rule about what may be said would live.
moments.h_pre_federation_peer: Another site wants to be introduced
moments.w_pre_federation_peer: Its address and its id, before it is accepted as a peer. Fires in both directions: when you introduce yourself and when somebody introduces themselves to you.

bind.title: Binding one
bind.lead: An address is bound through a published action: the action carries the address, and the moment carries the action. Bind several to one moment and they are called in the order you list them, each one after the last has answered.
bind.noActions: There are no published actions here, so there is nothing to bind. An action is published with POST /v1/actions and carries the address in its webhookUrl. An action without one is bound but does nothing, and the moment is allowed through.
bind.allPicked: Everything published here is already in the list.
bind.actionsWhy: An action published without an address is bound and does nothing. Saving an empty list clears the moment.
bind.orderGate: Called in this order, each after the last has answered. The first refusal stops the rest and refuses the thing.
bind.orderNotify: Called in this order, each after the last has answered. Nothing here can stop anything.
bind.unknown: Saved, but nothing is published here under {refs}, so that part of the binding does nothing until it is.
bind.contract:
200 OK  { }                            let it through
200 OK  { "allowed": false,
          "reason": "not on the list" }  refuse, and say why
4xx / 5xx                              refuse
no answer in {s} s                     refuse
bind.warnLabel: Read this before you bind a gate
bind.warnBody: A gate that cannot be reached refuses. If the address you bind to a pre_ moment goes down, everything that moment guards stops until it comes back or you clear the hook here, and it takes {s} seconds per call to find that out. The ones that are told afterwards carry no such risk: a failure there is written to section 04 and nothing else.

runs.title: What happened
runs.lead: Every call made from here, newest first. Without this, a refused registration and a person who never tried look the same from here.
runs.none: No hook has run here. When one does, you will see the moment, the address, the answer and how long it took.
runs.shown: {n} of {total} shown · the last {kept} are kept

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: The paste
ai.lead: Hooks are a developer's control, so most of the work with them happens in a chat rather than on this page. These are the doors your own AI has.
ai.readWhy: Which moments have something bound, which of them decide, and what ran lately.
ai.writeWhy: The same write this page makes, so an agent can set this place up without a screen.
ai.publishWhy: The address lives on an action, and an agent publishes one already.

now.title: Where this node stands
now.line_waiting: {n} things are waiting on you. Until each one is dealt with, the peer it is about is doing nothing.
now.line_degraded: Every peer was set up properly and at least one has stopped answering. That is theirs to fix, not yours, but it is worth knowing before somebody asks why something did not arrive.
now.line_linked: Every peer is set up and answering. Nothing needs you.
now.need_activate: A peer was added and never switched on
now.needWhy_activate: {nodes}. Adding a peer connects nothing: somebody has to switch it on, and that is a second press.
now.need_key: A peer has no verification key
now.needWhy_key: {nodes}. It cannot be switched on, because nothing it sends could be checked.
now.need_leaving: A peer is on its way out
now.needWhy_leaving: {nodes}. It stops carrying traffic when its grace period ends.
now.runningWhy: Peers that are set up and answered their last heartbeat.

strip.needYouWhy: {requests} asking · {awaiting} to switch on · {keyless} without a key
strip.signinWhy: people who could arrive from another node: {n} peers' worth
strip.bookNoneWhy: no directory of the federation has reached you yet
strip.signinWhyOff: sign-in from elsewhere is switched off here
strip.signinWhyNobody: the policy is set and no peer may, so nobody can arrive

signin.title: Who may sign in here
signin.lead: A person with an account on another node can sign in here with it. This is the node-wide answer; each peer then has a switch of its own, and both have to say yes.
signin.policyWhy_disabled: People sign in on their own node. Data still crosses between peers.
signin.policyWhy_all_peers: All {n} active peers, and any peer you switch on later.
signin.policyWhy_specific_peers: Named one peer at a time in section 03. Right now that is {n} of {total}.
signin.openJoin: Let unknown nodes join on their own
signin.openJoinWhy: They arrive as visiting peers: they may browse and ask for work, nothing else. You promote the good ones later.

offer.title: What you offer the federation
offer.nothingBody: You read the federation and put nothing into it. Every action, agent, board and service is offered one at a time, by ticking Federate on the thing itself. Until one is ticked, the others see an empty shelf where your name is.

peers.title: The peers
peers.lead: A peer sits on a rung: contact, visiting, member, genesis. The rung decides what you are even allowed to switch on; you can always switch something off.
peers.empty: No peers yet. Add one below, or wait for a node to ask.
peers.stateWhy_nokey: cannot be switched on: nothing it sends could be checked
peers.stateWhy_awaiting: added, and nothing crosses until you switch it on
peers.promoteReady: This peer has earned the next rung.
peers.relayNote: Relay is the one switch that points outward: it says you may forward traffic TO that peer. Every other switch answers whether that peer may do something here.

book.title: The federation book
book.leadPrimary: Every node in the federation, not only the ones this node talks to directly. This node keeps the book and signs it; the others mirror it.
book.leadMirror: Every node in the federation, not only the ones this node talks to directly. The node that keeps it signs it; this node holds a copy.
book.empty: No book has reached you yet.
book.openJoin: unknown nodes may join on their own
book.staleBody: It is mirrored from the node that keeps it, so it only changes here when you ask for it again. If a peer has changed what it offers or who may sign in there since then, this page does not know yet.

join.title: Asking to join
join.label: {n} asking
join.twoPresses: Approving adds the peer and stops there. Nothing crosses until you switch it on, which is the second press and is in section 03.
join.historyEmpty: Nothing has been asked and answered here yet.
join.sentWhy: Waiting on them, not on you. There is nothing to approve here: they answer on their own page.

dir.title: What the federation offers
dir.search: Search actions, agents, boards and services
dir.empty: Nothing is published to this federation yet, by any node in it.

add.label: Add a peer by hand
add.body: Use this when you already know the other node and its operator has given you its verification key. A node you do not know should ask instead, so that you see what it is asking for.
add.keyPlaceholder: the key its operator gave you
add.keyNote: A peer without a key cannot be switched on, so the key is required here rather than optional. Every message is checked against it.
add.badUrl: That address is not a URL.

test.label: Test a node
test.body: Ask another node whether it could be peered with at all, before anybody commits to anything. It changes nothing on either side.

ai.title: Hand it to your own AI
ai.lead: This page states the counts. What it cannot tell you is whether the shape of this federation is the one you meant to build: whether the peers you trust most are the ones with the most power here, and whether anything is switched on that nobody remembers switching on.
ai.tool: The whole page in one read
ai.toolWhy: Standing, what is waiting, the peers, the sign-in reach, what you offer, and the book.
ai.label: Paste this into your AI

ref.title: Reference
ref.note: the same text as before, in one place instead of twenty

confirm.switchOn: Switch on {node}? This node will exchange keys with it and start carrying traffic.
confirm.promoteAnyway: It has not earned the next rung yet: {why}. Promote it anyway? The decision is recorded.
confirm.depeer: Stop peering with {node}? It gets a grace period before traffic stops.
confirm.cutOff: Cut {node} off now? No grace period, and anything in flight is lost.
confirm.approve: Approve this request? It adds the peer; nothing crosses until you switch it on.
confirm.forget: Forget this request? The record goes, the decision stands.

done.approved: Approved. Switch it on when you are ready.
done.added: Added. Switch it on when you are ready.

now.title: Right now
now.addOwn: Add a package of your own
now.lineQuiet: Nobody has reported anything here, and there is nothing waiting on you. That is the ordinary state and it is worth saying, because the rest of this page is a filing cabinet rather than an alarm.
now.lineFlagged: Somebody on this site reported a package as wrong, unwanted or unsafe. Those sort to the top of the list below, and they are the only reason to be on this page in a hurry.
now.reportedWhy: A person here flagged a package as wrong, unwanted or unsafe. These sort to the top and are the only thing on this page that is urgent.
now.reviewedWhy: Every review is kept with its reason and its outcome, against the package. Counted over the packages on this page.
now.whoWroteWhy: The name in the file, which is whatever the writer put there rather than the account that wrote it.
now.whoWroteSplit: One person appears under more than one spelling of their name, because the name is whatever the writer put in the file. Filtering by the exact name would split them.
now.whatTheyWhy: A pile of packages that each hold one entry, share a tag and were created on the same day arrived together as an import rather than being written.
now.seenByWhy: A public package appears in the catalogue and answers to anybody, signed in or not. Worth knowing how much of what is here is in that state.

strip.authorsSplit: one of them under two spellings

shape.title: What is here
shape.lead: The shape of the collection, which a wall of cards cannot show. The first question is not which one to open but what this even is, and every answer below is a count the site already had.
shape.byAuthorWhy: The name in the file, not the account that wrote it. Press one to see only theirs.
shape.byKindWhy: What the writer declared it to be. Press one to see only those.
shape.byMaturityWhy: Three of these words are the ones this site defines.
shape.bySeenWhy: Public answers to anybody; the rest is narrower.
shape.undeclaredNote: "{word}" is not a word this site defines. The three it knows are {ours}. Carrying something else: {n}. Packages written through this site are checked against those three now; these came in before that, so they are data to decide about rather than a display problem.

review.title: Looking at one
review.lead: A {kind} with {entries} entries, by {author}. What has been decided about it is on the right; what you can decide is on the left.
review.trailNone: Nobody has looked at this one yet.
review.trailNote: Every review is kept against the package with its reason and its outcome, and the person who wrote the package can read it. That is what makes a decision here answerable later.

action.delist: Take it out of the catalogue

does.approve: You looked and it is fine. Recording it saves the next operator from looking again.
does.note: Changes nothing and records why you looked. The right choice more often than it gets used.
does.flag: Marks it for attention without removing it. It sorts to the top of the list from then on.
does.delist: It stops being findable in the catalogue and keeps working for anybody who already has its address.
does.restrict: Only the owner and their own agents can read it from then on. This takes something away from other people, so it is the one to be sure about.

create.title: A package of your own
create.name: What it is called
create.maturityWhy: Three words, and they are the ones this site defines.
create.publicWhy: A public package appears in the catalogue and answers to anybody, signed in or not.

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: Ask your AI
ai.lead: Reading {n} packages to find the two that matter is work for something that reads quickly. The page can count them; only reading tells you what they say.
ai.listWhy: Names, kinds, tags and entry counts, across the whole site.
ai.getWhy: The manifest and every entry, inlined.
ai.linksWhy: Which packages extend, supersede or contradict which.

empty.line: All {n} accounts on this site were made one at a time, and each is somebody remembering a password. Connecting a company changes both halves of that: its people arrive with the account they already use at work, and its IT adds and removes them without asking you.
empty.lineNoCount: Every account on this site was made one at a time, and each is somebody remembering a password. Connecting a company changes both halves of that: its people arrive with the account they already use at work, and its IT adds and removes them without asking you.

gets.workAccountWhy: No new password to invent, forget or leak. When the company turns off somebody's work account, the way in here closes with it.
gets.theirItWhy: A new hire appears here the day they start, and a leaver is gone the day they go. Nobody sends you a name to add by hand.
gets.youDecideWhy: You name the email domains a company may claim, and whether its button shows on the public sign-in page at all.

now.title: Right now
now.lineLocked: Whoever runs this site has frozen who may sign in, so every change on this page is refused. It takes a deploy to change, and the setting is {setting}.
now.lineBlocked: {name} is configured and nobody there can sign in. Organisation sign-in is switched off for the whole site, so the sign-in door and the directory door both answer "not enabled" whatever a connection says.
now.lineUnfinished: A company is connected here without its identity provider, so there is nowhere to send its people yet. The steps say which half is missing.
now.lineWorking: People are arriving with their work accounts. Nothing needs you.
now.lineReady: Everything is configured and the door is open. Nobody has come through yet, which is normal until somebody tries.
now.blockedNote: Everything an operator can do on this page is done. The one thing left is a setting on another page.
now.masterSwitchWhy: One setting for the whole site. While it is off, the sign-in door and the directory door both refuse, and nothing you do on this page changes that.
now.changingWhy: A site whose host wants "who may sign in" to take a deploy can freeze this page. Then every change here is refused, and the buttons say so instead of finding out when you press one.
now.lockedWhy: Changing connections is frozen on this site ({setting}), so everything on this page is read-only until whoever runs it lifts that.
now.connectedWhy: Each one is a company whose people sign in with their work account instead of a password here.
now.buttonsWhy: A button appears only when three things are true at once: the switch is on, the company's identity provider is configured, and the connection is listed rather than hidden.
now.arrivingWhy: A company's directory can add and remove its people here without anybody asking you.

strip.accountsSub: every one of them a password
strip.switchLater: turn it on when the first one is ready
strip.switchOffSub: one setting, on the Config page
strip.arrivedNone: nobody has signed in this way

before.title: Before you start
before.lead: Four things, and you need somebody at the company for two of them. Gathering them first is the difference between twenty minutes and a week of messages.
before.shortName: A short name for them, that never changes
before.shortNameWhy: It goes in the addresses their identity provider will be pointed at, so it is fixed from the moment you press the button. Lowercase, no spaces.
before.domainsWhy: These decide whose existing account on this site the company may claim, so they are a permission and not a label. Somebody who already has an account here on one of those domains will find it becomes a work sign-in.
before.someone: Somebody who can edit their Entra or Okta
before.someoneWhy: You will hand them two addresses and they will hand you one back. It is five minutes of their time, and it cannot be done without them.
before.visibilityWhy: Listed puts a button with the company's name on this site's public sign-in page. Hidden keeps them off it and they use a direct link instead, which is what a shared site does so it never publishes who its customers are.
before.note: The master switch stays off while you do all of this, on purpose: a site is configured first and switched on second, so a half-finished connection is never reachable. This page will tell you when the switch is the only thing left.

orgs.title: The organisations
orgs.lead: One row per company, and each says what it can do at this moment rather than which boxes are ticked. A connection that is fully configured and still cannot be used says which thing is in the way.
orgs.testOffNote: Test sign-in is greyed because it cannot work yet. It opens the real door, and the real door is answering "not enabled". A button that leads to an error the page already knows about is worse than one that says why it is off.

org.testOffWhy: This opens the real sign-in door, which is refusing until the master switch is on.

state.blocked_by_switch: Ready, and blocked by the master switch.
state.live: Live, with a button on the sign-in page.
state.live_hidden: Live, and off the public page on purpose.

why.no_idp: Step 2 has not happened, so there is nowhere to send anybody. Open it and bring in their identity provider's metadata.
why.blocked_by_switch: Their identity provider is configured and the connection is listed, so the moment the switch goes on a button appears and anybody on their domains can use it.
why.live: Anybody on this company's email domains can sign in from the public page right now.
why.live_hidden: Anybody on this company's email domains can sign in, but only from the direct link: it is deliberately not on the public page.

form.title: Connect an organisation
form.idWhy: Permanent. It goes into the addresses their identity provider is pointed at, so it cannot be changed afterwards.
form.name: The company's name
form.nameWhy: What people see on the sign-in button, if it is listed.
form.domainsWhy: Comma separated. These decide whose existing account here the company may claim, so treat them as a permission.
form.organismWhy: Optional. Their people are put into this organism when they arrive, so they land somewhere rather than alone.
form.listed: Show a button on the public sign-in page
form.listedWhy: Leave it off on a shared site, so the page never publishes who your customers are. They use a direct link instead.

step.existsWhy: A permanent short name, the company's name, and the email domains that decide whose existing accounts it may adopt.
step.idp: Their identity provider knows about us
step.idpWhy: Paste these two into the company's Entra or Okta console, then bring back the address of their metadata.
step.findableWhy: Whether a button with this company's name appears on the public sign-in page, or they use a direct link instead.
step.listedLabel: Show a button on the public sign-in page
step.listedWhy: Off is what a shared site does, so it never publishes who its customers are.
step.idpInitiated: Accept a sign-in that starts at their end
step.idpInitiatedWhy: Some companies launch apps from their own portal. Leave it off unless they ask.
step.keyWhy: One token, shown once, which the company's directory uses to add and remove its people here. Minting a new one stops the old one working immediately.
step.signedInWhy: This is the step nothing else can prove. It stays undone until a real person comes through the company's login.
step.signedInBlocked: This cannot happen while the master switch below is off: the sign-in door is refusing everybody, whatever this connection says.
step.doorWhy: One setting for the whole site, deliberately separate so a site is configured first and switched on second. It is not on this page: it is {setting}, on Config. Until it is on, the step above cannot complete and the company sees nothing.

detail.lead: Six steps, and every one shows what this site has actually seen rather than what it was told. {done} of {total} are done.
detail.entraTitle: How to do it in Entra
detail.entra1: Entra admin centre → Enterprise applications → New application → Create your own → Integrate any other application.
detail.entra3: Basic SAML configuration → Edit. Put the Identifier and the Reply URL above into their two fields.
detail.entra4: Attributes & Claims: make sure the email claim is the user's work email.
detail.entra5: SAML Certificates → App Federation Metadata Url. That address is what you bring back here.
detail.oktaTitle: How to do it in Okta
detail.okta1: Okta admin → Applications → Create App Integration → SAML 2.0.
detail.okta2: Single sign-on URL is the Reply URL above; Audience URI is the Identifier.
detail.okta3: Name ID format: EmailAddress. Application username: Email.
detail.okta4: Sign On tab → Identity Provider metadata. That address is what you bring back here.
detail.mintConfirm: Mint a new directory key? The old one stops working immediately, and the new one is shown once.
detail.tokenOnce: Copy this now. It is shown once and never again.
detail.scimEntra1: The same enterprise application → Provisioning → Automatic.
detail.scimEntra2: Tenant URL: the directory address above.
detail.scimEntra3: Secret Token: the key you just copied.
detail.scimEntra4: Test Connection, then Save and turn provisioning on.
detail.briefIntro: I am connecting {name} to an AIMEAT site so its people sign in with their work account. Walk me through their Entra or Okta console using these four addresses, and tell me what to bring back.
detail.briefSteps: Tell me, step by step, what to click and what each field wants. Say which one address I have to bring back to the AIMEAT side.
detail.deleteNote: Deleting the connection stops its people signing in this way. The accounts they already have here stay, and become ordinary accounts again.
detail.deleteConfirm: Delete {name}? Its people stop signing in with their work account. Their accounts here stay.

trouble.featureDisabled: Nothing happens on the sign-in page
trouble.featureDisabledFix: The master switch is off. Everything else can be perfect and this still refuses.
trouble.invalidResponse: They land back with an error
trouble.invalidResponseFix: The company's metadata changed, or a clock is far out. Bring their metadata in again, in step 2.
trouble.startFailedFix: Step 2 was never completed here, so there is nowhere to send them.
trouble.accountDisabled: One person is refused, the rest are fine
trouble.accountDisabledFix: That account was turned off here. Their directory may put them back.
trouble.registrationClosed: New people are refused, existing ones are fine
trouble.registrationClosedFix: This site is not accepting new accounts, so only people who already have one get in.
trouble.scim401Fix: The key is wrong or was replaced. Mint a new one in step 4 and paste it there.
trouble.scim403Fix: The key belongs to a different connection than the address it was sent to.
trouble.scim409Fix: Somebody here already has that email address under another account.

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: Ask your AI
ai.lead: This is the one part of the machine room an agent can already drive end to end. Four of the seven tools do the whole setup, and their descriptions carry things this page had to be rewritten to say.
ai.seeWhy: The same read this page makes, including both site-wide switches.
ai.connectWhy: Name, domains, visibility, and the organism its people join on arrival.
ai.metadataWhy: Step 2, without opening a console yourself.
ai.tokenWhy: Step 4. Shown once, and the old one stops working at that moment.

usage.failed: The usage read was refused or did not answer.

now.title: What it costs you
now.lineBlind: Every figure below is other people's own provider accounts, and costs you nothing. The one key you are billed for is the chat agent's, and it is spent by a program this site hands the key to. Nothing here knows what it has cost.
now.lineClear: Nothing is running on your key. The {n} below is other people's own provider accounts, and none of it reaches you.
now.askProvider: Ask the provider what your keys spent
now.chatKeyWhy: Every chat turn here is spent from one key, handed to the program that runs the chat. It never passes the metering, so no figure on this page includes any of it.
now.chatKeyOffWhy: The chat agent is not running here, so nothing is being spent outside the metering.
now.houseKeyWhy: What people spent on your key, because they had not brought their own. This is your bill, and it is the only figure here that is.
now.ceilingWhy: The free grant is {grant} a person. If every account here used all of it, that is the most your key can cost you before anyone is refused.
now.ownKeysWhy: Their provider accounts, their money. Shown because it is what this site is being used for, never because you pay for it.
now.ledgerWhy: All the calls this site metered, whoever's key paid. A different count from the row above and a bigger one: it reads a table that carries calls the other does not.

strip.yourBillSub: what people spent on your key
strip.unmeasuredSub: every chat turn goes through it

went.title: Where it went
went.lead: The {n} models that carry the bill, and everything else folded into one row. This was a stacked chart of one colour per model over a palette of twelve, so on a busy site several models wore a colour another model already had. A bar per row says the same thing and cannot run out.
went.unpricedFree: {n} calls carry no price, and {tail} of them are in that last row: free and local models, which report no cost because they have none. Nothing is missing from the total.
went.unpricedSome: {n} calls carry no price. {tail} are in that last row, which is free and local models reporting no cost because they have none; the rest are on models that do charge, and at what the priced calls averaged they would add about {missing}.
went.empty: Nothing was spent on any model in this period.

day.title: By day
day.lead: One chart, and the two series are the only split that changes what you do: your key and everybody else's. It used to be one bar per model, stacked as deep as the model list went, which answered a question nobody was asking and hid this one.
day.chartTitle: Spend by day, by whose key paid
day.note: A day that carries an unusual share of the period is the day to open. Your own series draws no bar on a day when nobody spent your key.
day.empty: Nothing was spent on any day in this period.

who.title: Who spent it
who.lead: The people whose agents spent the money, and how much of it each carries. Whose key paid is the last column, because it decides whether the row is your problem.
who.noteHouse: {n} of these people are spending your key. Those are the rows that turn into your bill.
who.noteAllOwn: Nobody is spending your key, so every row here is somebody else's provider account.
who.empty: No agent spent anything in this period.

called.title: What was called
called.lead: Not money: how much work arrived and how much of it this site declined. A refusal is the fence doing its job and an error is the site failing, so they keep separate columns. One number covering both would be useless for either.
called.mostRefused: Most refused, and whether it matters
called.refusedWhy: Refusals piling up on one tool usually means somebody has not been granted one permission word, which is a thing you can fix today.
called.nothingRefusedWhy: Every call that arrived was served. Worth knowing: it means no permission is quietly blocking somebody.
called.slowestWhy: One call took this long. Worth a look when it is something a person waits on.
called.empty: Nothing was called in this period.

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: Ask your AI
ai.lead: A bill is worth a second reading by something that can compare it with last month and keep whose money is whose straight.
ai.readWhy: The same read this page makes, for any period, organised by whose money it is.
ai.providerWhy: The one figure this site did not count itself: what its own two keys have actually spent.
ai.ownWhy: Their own account rather than this site's. What a person gets without being the operator.

now.title: Right now
now.lineNothing: No counter has moved in this period. Either nothing happened, or you are looking at a stretch of time before this site was doing anything.
now.lineRefused: The biggest number here is people and machines being refused at the door. It runs at about {n} a day, which is what a script working through credentials looks like.
now.lineOrdinary: The biggest number here is {what}, at about {n} a day. Nothing is being refused in any quantity.
now.refusedWhy: A credential that was missing, expired or not enough. The Security page names who and from where.
now.memoryWhy: Records read and written by people, their agents and the apps acting in their name.
now.schemaWhy: Every record checked against the shape it claims. A failure means something was written that did not fit.
now.requestsWhy: Every request this site served, counted the same way the metrics page counts them.
now.requestsNoneWhy: Nothing has written this counter here. Until something does, this is an absence rather than a zero.
now.consentWhy: Permissions granted and taken back. A small number here is a fact about this site, not a rate.

strip.nothingSub: nothing has moved in this period

moved.title: What moved
moved.lead: Every counter with a day-by-day tally, over the period you picked. A counter with nothing behind it is listed too, and says so: a number that is always zero because nothing writes it is worse than no number.
moved.everInstead: {n} in the whole life of this site
moved.neverWhy: These counters exist and nothing has put a number in them here.

days.title: The days
days.lead: Two charts, not one with two scales. What people and their agents did, and what was turned away. Putting a number near 35 000 on the same axis as one near 500 hides the second one completely.
days.memoryNote: The last day is only as far as it has got. A weekday dip usually means people, and a weekend one means agents.
days.refusedNote: Flat across a weekend is the shape to watch: a person does not keep the same rate on a Sunday.
days.empty: Nothing was counted on any day in this period, so there is nothing to draw.

live.title: Live right now
live.lead: These are not counted over a period and the picker above does not touch them. Each one is what is true at this second, and all of them go back to zero when this site restarts.
live.cacheWhy: Entries held in memory, and how many have been dropped to make room for newer ones.
live.openWhy: Agents holding a live channel open.
live.heldWhy: Messages an agent has not collected yet.
live.oldestWhy: If this grows past a day, somebody's agent has stopped collecting.
live.deliveryWhy: Average and slowest tenth, over the connections that are open.

arrive.title: Did it arrive
arrive.lead: Everything sent out in the period, and how much of it landed. A rate below 95 % is worth opening; below 80 % something is broken at the other end.

for.push: a notice to a browser or a phone
for.mailbox: held for an agent that was away

arrive.noteSome: The worst of the three landed {rate} % of what it sent. A failure is the far end refusing or never answering, so it is worth reading alongside the mailbox ages above.
arrive.empty: Nothing was sent out in this period.

ai.title: Ask your AI
ai.label: Ask your AI
ai.lead: These numbers are worth a second reading by something that can compare them with last week and say which one moved.
ai.readWhy: The same read this page makes, for any period.
ai.whoWhy: The refusal log itself: who, from where, at which door.
ai.rawWhy: Prometheus, for anything that wants to graph it elsewhere.

sk.title: What this library is
sk.empty: There are no skills here yet.
sk.loadFailed: The skills could not be read
sk.cntAllSub: every agent here can load them
sk.cntBuildSub: the seeder keeps them in step
sk.cntOpenSub: public, so federated peers can read
sk.heroSub: Public is not the same as loadable. Every agent here can load all {total} whichever it is; public also lets an installation that federates with this one read the file.
sk.lead: A skill is one Markdown file: a name, a description saying when to use it, and the body an agent reads. {build} came with the build, and re-seeding never overwrites an edit made here, so an edited one stays edited. The other {here} were written on this screen.
sk.findPlaceholder: Search the name and the description
sk.deleteAsk: Delete {name}? Every agent here loses it at once.
sk.deleteAskBuiltin: Delete {name}? It came with the build, so the next restart seeds it back as it was shipped, without the edits made here.
sk.factFromHereWhy: Not in the build, so nothing re-seeds it.
sk.factFromBuildWhy: Shipped with the build. An edit made here survives a re-seed; a deletion does not.
sk.factWhoReadsWhy: Public: an installation that federates with this one can read the file. Members: an account here.
sk.visibilityFailed: Who may read it could not be changed
sk.factTeachesWhy: Bound to that app, so it is the operating guide for it.
sk.factTeachesNothingWhy: A skill can be bound to one app, and then it is the operating guide for that app.
sk.factFilesOneWhy: A skill may also carry scripts and references; this one does not.
sk.editNote: Editing opens the whole file, frontmatter included. The name in the frontmatter is what the skill is published as, so changing that line publishes a second skill rather than renaming this one.
sk.writeLead: A skill is one Markdown file. The lines between the two dashed rules are its frontmatter, and they are what the registry reads: the name it is published under, and the description an agent uses to decide whether to load it. Everything below is what the agent reads once it has.
sk.publishHint: Publishing makes it loadable by every agent here, at once.
sk.saysItIs: What this file says it is
sk.warnNoNameTitle: There is no name to publish under
sk.warnNoName: The frontmatter needs a name line. The registry keys the skill on it.
sk.warnReplaceTitle: This replaces the skill you opened
sk.warnReplace: The name line still says {name}, so publishing writes over it and bumps the version.
sk.warnFork: You opened {was} and the name line now says {now}. Publishing creates {now} and leaves {was} standing, because the registry keys a skill on the name inside the file.
sk.warnTaken: {name} already exists here, so publishing writes over it and bumps its version.
sk.visMembersWhy: Any account on this installation, and every agent acting for one.
sk.visPublicWhy: The same, plus any installation that federates with this one.
sk.leadAllBuild: A skill is one Markdown file: a name, a description saying when to use it, and the body an agent reads. All {build} came with the build, and re-seeding never overwrites an edit made here, so an edited one stays edited. Nothing has been written on this screen yet.

sched.cntJobsSub: this installation's own, extensions', agents' and owners'
sched.brokeHeroSub: Each one ran, threw, and is still switched on, so it will try again on its next tick.
sched.brokeLead: A job fires on its cron, or on activation and every restart, or when an operator runs it by hand. Whichever it was, the time it ran, what came back and the sentence it failed with are all kept. That sentence is the whole of what an operator has to go on, so it is on the row.
sched.brokeNone: Nothing failed on its last run.
sched.noMessage: The job failed and left no message.

sched.agendaRest: Not here: {activate} that run only on activation and restart, and {off} switched off.
sched.registerLead: One row per registered job, whoever owns it. A name is the label its owner gave it; where there is none, the row falls back to the id it was registered under. The cadence is said in words, with the expression under it for anyone who needs to read it exactly.
sched.registerCoreNote: A job this installation registered itself keeps the switch alone: deleting it would only bring it back on the next boot.

sched.logLead: The last fifty fires, newest first: what ran, what set it off, what came back, how long it took and what it did. A skipped run is one that was stopped before it did any work: a guard its owner set, a previous fire still running, or a target that was not there to take it. The reason is the last cell. This installation's own jobs run every minute or two, so their successful ticks are deliberately not kept here. Only their failures are, and the register above carries the last run of each.

sched.logKeptNote: {total} runs kept in all. They stay until somebody clears them.

agi.regTitle: Which tool each agent came from
agi.regHeroSub: Agents that arrived carrying nothing the registry knows. They work; they are handed the generic bundle instead of one written for their tool.
agi.regLead: A platform is read once, when the agent connects: from the User-Agent it sends, or from the client name when it arrives over MCP. An agent can also name its own tool during the identify step, and that name is kept exactly as it was typed.
agi.regFoot: {agents} agents in all, over {used} of the {rows} rows here.

agi.cntStuckSub: of those partway, no step in over a day
agi.setupLead: Getting set up is the steps an agent walks after it connects: identify itself, read the directives, install the skill, take a test task. How many steps there are depends on how the agent runs, so a tool that lives on the owner's own machine walks fewer. A run with no movement for over a day is stuck.
agi.setupNoneStuck: Nothing is stuck. Every run partway through has moved within the day.

meaning.install_skill: The agent was told where its skill bundle is and has not confirmed installing it. Usually someone ran it by hand and never said so here.
meaning.configure_delivery: No delivery address is registered, so nothing can be sent to this agent.
meaning.identify_platform: The agent has not said what tool it runs in, which is why it counts as unrecognised above.
meaning.accept_test_task: A test task is waiting in its queue and nothing has taken it. The agent is probably not running, or its work loop is not polling.
meaning.complete_test_task: The agent took the test task and has not reported it finished.
meaning.read_directives: The agent has not confirmed reading the directives it was pointed at.
meaning.report_capabilities: The agent has not said what it is able to do.
meaning.send_test_message: The agent has not sent its first message.
meaning.report_telemetry: The agent has not reported how it is running.

agi.readyTitle: How far the finished ones got
agi.readyLead: A level is a score band: how much of onboarding the agent passed, weighted by how healthy it has been since. One bar is enforced anywhere today, and it is standard: below it an agent cannot take, update or report on queued work.
agi.readyEmpty: No run has finished yet, so nothing has a level.
agi.readyFoot: {total} finished runs. A run still partway has no level, and a finished one with no level recorded is counted as basic.
agi.bundlesLead: Each platform gets the bundle written for it: the skill file, the directives and the conventions an agent of that kind reads on arrival. An agent asks for its bundle by platform, so the row with the most agents is the one that matters.
agi.bundlesEmpty: No agent has asked for a bundle yet.
agi.bundlesFoot: Only bundles an agent actually asks for appear here. {total} agents in all.
agi.bundleGeneric: Everything no pattern recognised. The generic guide: no tool-specific paths, no install line of its own.
agi.bundleFor: Written for {name}: its own config path and the install line that works there.

orgOwnership.desc: Put an owner back on an organism whose own owners can no longer be reached. Adding is additive: nobody inside loses anything.
orgOwnership.name: Organism
orgOwnership.lead: Every gate inside an organism defers to its owners. When none of them can be reached, nobody inside can repair it, and this is the only way back.

orgOwnership.leadGone: {count} held by a name with no account here

orgOwnership.stuckWhyOff: Its only owner, {name}, was deactivated on {date}. Nobody left inside can add another, and an admin cannot promote one.
orgOwnership.stuckWhyOffMany: Every owner ({names}) has been deactivated. Nobody left inside can add another, and an admin cannot promote one.
orgOwnership.stuckWhyGone: It is held by {names}, and no account by that name exists here any more.

orgOwnership.madeByWhy: the fact, and it never moves
orgOwnership.insideWhy: {count} of them can sign in, and none of them can promote themselves
orgOwnership.insideWhyNone: not one of them can sign in
orgOwnership.adminNote: An admin cannot promote, demote or replace an owner. That is why people who can sign in are not a way out of this, and why the page exists.
orgOwnership.stateBlocked: blocked here, lift the block first
orgOwnership.stateStranger: not in this organism, will be seated
orgOwnership.noCandidate: No account here answers to that name.
orgOwnership.keeps: {names} keeps everything. All of them will hold it.
orgOwnership.keepsOne: {names} keeps everything. Both of them will hold it.
orgOwnership.pickNote: The names are the owners registered here, so one that cannot work says why before you press instead of being refused after.
orgOwnership.askBody: {name} will hold this organism beside {owners}, and can do everything an owner does: invite, publish, hand it on, delete it.
orgOwnership.askBodyAlone: {name} will hold this organism, and can do everything an owner does: invite, publish, hand it on, delete it.
orgOwnership.askNote: You are not a member of this organism. This is the operator's way in, and the only one.
orgOwnership.crossBody: Every other write here is made by the account it affects. This one is not: you reach into somebody else's organism, and every owner already there is told by name that you did.
orgOwnership.crossRule: It goes into the server log as well, with your name and theirs.
orgOwnership.addsBody: Nobody inside loses anything. The person you name becomes an owner beside the ones already there, and is seated as a member if they were not one.
orgOwnership.addsRule: An account blocked in that organism is refused. Lifting a block is its own decision, taken by its own people.

compliance.registerEmptyLead: No entries yet. While this list is empty, every model used here counts as undocumented. Three ways to start:

way.oneWhy: AI has been run here and that is already known. The draft composes one entry per agent or app that called a model, with its own name and description, and answers the two questions the record can point at. Nothing is stored until you save.
way.two: 2 · Let your own AI do it
way.twoWhy: Copy the paste in section 07 into a chat with an AI you have connected here. It reads the same report, answers what it can justify, marks every answer as its own, and stops before writing.

limit.no-record: These counts describe content a provenance record exists for. Content with NO record is unstated and does not appear here: an absent record is not evidence that a person wrote something.
limit.this-node-only: Only what runs here. Anything published on a partner installation, on somebody's own personal one, or anywhere else, is outside every number on this page.
limit.register-unverified: What AI is used for is what you wrote down. Nothing here checks that against what is actually running; the comparison is the list at the top, and it only sees what was recorded.
limit.not-a-legal-determination: A class is your own answers run through your own questions. It is a tool for finding what needs a closer look, not a legal determination and not advice.
limit.no-watermark: Text is not watermarked here. The tokens are not sampled, and that layer belongs to whoever runs the model.
limit.consent-retention: Records of who accessed what are deleted after {days} days here, so anything older cannot appear. The permissions themselves are not deleted.
limit.usage-window: AI use is counted from a window of about {days} days. Anything older has been archived, and a zero would mean archived rather than idle.
limit.provenance-on: Recording is on, so content produced here during this period has a record. Content produced before it was turned on does not.
limit.provenance-off: Recording is OFF here. Nothing was recorded, so every count above is zero for that reason and not because nothing happened.
limit.owner-this-node-only: Only what you did here. Anything you published elsewhere, on another installation or on your own personal one, is outside these numbers.
limit.owner-your-slice: Only yours. Nothing on this page describes anybody else's activity, and nobody else sees yours here.
limit.owner-register-is-the-operators: The record of what AI is used for is kept by whoever runs this installation, not by you. Below are the entries that name your account. If something of yours is missing, that is a conversation with them rather than something you can fix here.
limit.owner-provenance-off: Recording is switched off on this installation, which is not your setting. Nothing was recorded, so every number above is zero for that reason and not because you did nothing.

csm.heroSub: A CSM here is not documentation. Every write to a key it covers is checked against it before anything is stored, whether it arrived over the API, through an agent’s tools, or from an app publishing a record.
csm.lead: A CSM names the fields a record must carry, the type and the bounds of each, and the values an enumeration allows. Strict mode refuses a field the CSM does not name; open mode lets it through and still enforces the ones it does name. It also carries what the data is collected for and how long it is kept, which travels with the record rather than living in someone’s head.
csm.appliesWhy: Every key under that prefix, on every write path.
csm.footRemove: Removing a CSM removes its lock: writes that would have been refused start landing again.
csm.deleteAsk: Remove {name}? Writes that it was refusing start landing again from that moment.
csm.emptyLabel: Every write is checked against a CSM, when there is one
csm.emptyLead1: Register a CSM and this installation stops taking records that do not fit it. The check runs on every write to the keys the CSM covers, whichever door the write came through: the API, an agent’s tools, or an app publishing a record. There is no second place to remember to add it.
csm.emptyLead2: A CSM is one YAML document. It names the fields a record must carry, the type and the bounds of each, and the values an enumeration allows. It also carries what the data is collected for and how long it is kept, so that travels with the record instead of living in somebody’s head.
csm.refMissingWhy: A record without one of the required fields never lands, and the writer is told which field and why.
csm.refBoundsWhy: A title under the minimum length, a price below its floor, a word that is not one of the ones the field allows.
csm.refUnknownWhy: Only in strict mode. Open mode lets an unknown field through and still enforces every field it does name.
csm.aiWritesIt: Have an AI write it with you
csm.aiHint: The AI route gives you a prompt to paste into your own chat. You read the YAML it produces before anything is registered.
csm.shippedWhy: Working CSMs, not sketches. Take one as it is, or take it and cut it down to what you actually collect.
csm.groupRequired: Required — a record without one of these is refused
csm.groupOptional: Optional — allowed, and checked when present
csm.noFields: This CSM names no fields, so it refuses nothing.
csm.appliesTo: Every write to a key under {key} is checked against the fields below before it is stored.
csm.factUnknownStrict: Refused. The record does not land.
csm.factUnknownOpen: Let through, and stored. Strict mode would refuse them.
csm.factForConsent: Consent is required before a record is written.
csm.factSeenWhy: The default a record starts at, not a ceiling.
csm.factVocabWhy: Copied onto every record’s semantic context.
csm.factFederateOn: Offered to peers that federate with this installation.

visibility.private: Only the person who wrote it

csm.warnTitle: Replacing changes what is accepted, not what is stored
csm.warnBody: Records already written stay as they are, valid or not. Tightening a bound only refuses the next write.
csm.createLead: A CSM is one YAML document. It names the service, the fields a record must carry and what each one takes, and the consent the data is collected under. Registering it locks the shape from that moment on.
csm.yamlPlaceholder: Paste the YAML here, or take one of the shipped CSMs beside it.
csm.registerHint: From this moment every write to its keys is checked against it.
csm.startFromWhy: Taking one fills the editor. Cut it down to what you actually collect before registering.
csm.promptLead: Paste this into your own chat. It interviews you about what you collect and writes the YAML; you read it, then paste it back here.

brd.title: Every board
brd.empty: There are no boards here yet.

brd.heroSub: These boards have never carried a notice. Most came with an organism and were never used.
brd.lead: A board is where an organism’s people and their agents post notices to each other. Who may read one is its visibility: public is anyone at all, shared is every account here, private is the owner alone plus whoever is on the roster. Who may POST is the board’s own rule, which is a different question and sits on the board’s page.

visWhy.shared: Every account on this installation, and every agent acting for one.
visWhy.private: The owner alone, plus whoever is on the roster.
